Question 1
?

Consider the arc of the curve x=y3−6y2+9y that lies in the first quadrant between its y-intercepts. What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis?

a
π∫06y1+9(y2−4y+3)2dy
b
2π∫03y1+9(y2−4y+3)2dy
c
π∫06y1+(y2−4y+3)2dy
d
2π∫03y1+9(y3−6y2+9y)2dy
e
6π∫03y1+(y2−4y+3)2dy
Submit

decision.explanation: The y-intercepts satisfy y(y-3)^2=0, giving bounds 0 and 3. Rotation about the x-axis has radius y, so S=2π∫₀³ y√(1+(dx/dy)²) dy. Since dx/dy=3(y²-4y+3), this is option b.

after.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

$$

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{3}-6{y}^{2}+9y)=3{y}^{2}-12y+9.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

a
π∫06y1+9(y2−4y+3)2dy
b
2π∫03y1+9(y2−4y+3)2dy
c
π∫06y1+(y2−4y+3)2dy
d

Submit

$$

Consider the arc of the curve x=y2−y4 that lies in the first quadrant between its y-intercepts. What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis?

a
 2π∫02y1+16y4−16y4dy
b
 2π∫01y1+4y2−16y4+16y6dy
c
 2π∫02y1+4y2−8y4+8y6dy
d
 2π∫01(y2−y4)1+4y2−16y4+16y6dy
e
 2π∫01(y2−y4)1+4y2−16y4dy

decision.explanation: The first-quadrant arc runs from y=0 to y=1, since x=y²(1−y²)=0 at those endpoints. Rotation about the x-axis has radius y. With dx/dy=2y−4y³, the surface area is 2π∫₀¹ y√(1+(2y−4y³)²) dy. Expanding the square gives option b.

Consider the arc of the curve $x={y}^{2}-{y}^{4}$ that lies in the first quadrant between its $y$-intercepts. What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
after.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-{y}^{4} & =0 \\ {y}^{2}(1-{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ y & =0,\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=1.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2}-{y}^{4})=2y-4{y}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y\sqrt{1+{(2y-4{y}^{3})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y\sqrt{1+4{y}^{2}-16{y}^{4}+16{y}^{6}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3

Consider the arc of the curve x=y2−y4 that lies in the first quadrant between its y-intercepts. What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis?

a
 2π∫02y1+16y4−16y4dy
b
 2π∫01y1+4y2−16y4+16y6dy
c
 2π∫02y1+4y2−8y4+8y6dy
d
 2π∫01(y2−y4)1+4y2−16y4+16y6dy
e
 2π∫01(y2−y4)1+4y2−16y4dy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated 2π radians about the x-axis using the formula

S=∫2πyds.

Since we're given a curve in the form x=f(y), we have

ds=1+(dxdy)2dy. Therefore, we will use

S=2π∫y1y2y1+(dxdy)2dy.

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the y-axis by solving the following equation:

y2−y4=0y2(1−y2)=0y=0,±1

Hence, we need to integrate from y=0 to y=1.

Computing the derivative, we get dxdy=ddy(y2−y4)=2y−4y3.

Finally, we obtain

S=2π∫y1y2y1+(dxdy)2dy=2π∫01y1+(2y−4y3)2dy=2π∫01y1+4y2−16y4+16y6dy.

Consider the arc of the curve $x={y}^{2}-{y}^{4}$ that lies in the first quadrant between its $y$-intercepts. What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
content.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-{y}^{4} & =0 \\ {y}^{2}(1-{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ y & =0,\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=1.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{2}-{y}^{4})=2y-4{y}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y\sqrt{1+{(2y-4{y}^{3})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y\sqrt{1+4{y}^{2}-16{y}^{4}+16{y}^{6}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$
